builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
summary: Draft calibration replaces the raw, typically underconfident draft-model distribution used in speculative decoding with a post-hoc calibrated version (standard temperature scaling or token-wise calibration) that better matches the target distribution and raises token acceptance. It costs essentially nothing in memory or latency, adding only a temperature-fitting step over calibration data and negligible per-token computation, with no quality loss since target verification remains unchanged. It can fail if the draft-target pair is already well calibrated, if the fitted temperature does not transfer across tasks or sampling conditions, or if the serving stack does not use speculative decoding at all, in which case the technique has nothing to improve.
rationale: For teams already serving with speculative decoding, applying a single temperature parameter to the draft logits is a near-zero-cost change with a reported acceptance-rate gain, but its magnitude depends on the specific draft-target pair and workload, so it warrants a quick A/B measurement before production rollout.

claims.statement: Draft calibration replaces the raw, typically underconfident draft-model distribution used in speculative decoding with a post-hoc calibrated version (standard temperature scaling or token-wise calibration) that better matches the target distribution and raises token acceptance. It costs essentially nothing in memory or latency, adding only a temperature-fitting step over calibration data and negligible per-token computation, with no quality loss since target verification remains unchanged. It can fail if the draft-target pair is already well calibrated, if the fitted temperature does not transfer across tasks or sampling conditions, or if the serving stack does not use speculative decoding at all, in which case the technique has nothing to improve.
Post-hoc temperature scaling of the draft distribution improves acceptance length by up to approximately 10% at almost no additional cost, with corresponding throughput gains in serving analysis.
